extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and researchers in functional analysis / partial differential equations
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, equivalent characterizations, and fundamental properties of unbounded linear operators (graphs, closedness, domain/density), their adjoints, relations between ranges and kernels, closed-range and surjectivity characterizations, and the weak topology on Banach spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of unbounded linear operator
rubrics_metrics.description: An unbounded linear operator from E into F is a linear map A : D(A) ⊂ E → F defined on a linear subspace D(A) ⊂ E (the domain). One says A is bounded (continuous) if D(A) = E and ∃ c ≥ 0 such that ||Au|| ≤ c||u|| ∀u ∈ E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domain D(A) may be a proper subspace; boundedness requires domain = whole space and a uniform operator norm bound. The operator norm for bounded operators is defined by sup_{u≠0} ||Au||/||u||.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph, range, and kernel
rubrics_metrics.description: Graph G(A) = {[u, Au]; u ∈ D(A)} ⊂ E × F. Range R(A) = {Au; u ∈ D(A)} ⊂ F. Kernel N(A) = {u ∈ D(A); Au = 0} ⊂ E.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These set-theoretic objects are basic and used to express closedness (G(A) closed), orthogonality relations and many equivalences concerning ranges/kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed operator (graph-closedness and sequential criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A map A is said to be closed if G(A) is closed in E × F. To prove A is closed: take a sequence (u_n) in D(A) with u_n → u in E and A u_n → f in F; then show (a) u ∈ D(A) and (b) f = Au.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sequential test is the practical method. Note: it is not sufficient to consider sequences with u_n → 0 and A u_n → f (and then deduce f = 0); full convergence must be considered. If A is closed then N(A) is closed; R(A) need not be closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Densely defined operators
rubrics_metrics.description: An operator is densely defined if D(A) is dense in E. In practice most unbounded operators of interest are closed and densely defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density of D(A) is crucial for defining the adjoint A* via extension arguments (uniqueness of extension depends on density).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the adjoint A* (domain and construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A : D(A) ⊂ E → F densely defined, define D(A*) = {v ∈ F*; ∃ c ≥ 0 such that |⟨v, Au⟩| ≤ c||u|| ∀u ∈ D(A)}. For v ∈ D(A*), the linear functional g(u)=⟨v,Au⟩ on D(A) extends (by continuity / Hahn–Banach) uniquely to f ∈ E*, and A*v := f. Fundamental relation: ⟨v, Au⟩_{F*,F} = ⟨A*v, u⟩_{E*,E} ∀u ∈ D(A), ∀v ∈ D(A*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two constructions are noted: (i) extension by Hahn–Banach analytic form, or (ii) extension by continuity using density of D(A) (preferred when available). Uniqueness follows from density. D(A*) can be non-dense in pathological cases but is dense in weak-* topology if A is closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjoint of a bounded operator
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a bounded operator (D(A)=E), then A* is bounded (from F* into E*) and D(A*) = F*. Moreover ||A*||_{L(F*,E*)} = ||A||_{L(E,F)}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses the basic relation |⟨A*v,u⟩| = |⟨v,Au⟩| ≤ ||A||·||u||·||v|| to deduce boundedness and the norm equality via dual estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: A* is closed (Proposition 2.17)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A : D(A) ⊂ E → F is densely defined, then A* is closed: G(A*) is closed in F* × E*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses sequences v_n ∈ D(A*) with v_n → v in F* and A*v_n → f in E*, passing limits in the defining relation ⟨v_n, Au⟩ = ⟨A*v_n, u⟩ and using density to conclude v∈D(A*) and A*v = f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graph orthogonality relation between A and A*
rubrics_metrics.description: Let I : F* × E* → E* × F* be I([v,f]) = [−f, v]. Then I[G(A*)] = G(A)^{⊥} (i.e., the image of the graph of A* equals the orthogonal complement of the graph of A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relation is shown by translating the fundamental relation ⟨v,Au⟩ = ⟨A*v,u⟩ into the orthogonality condition −⟨f,u⟩ + ⟨v,Au⟩ = 0. It underlies subsequent orthogonality relations between ranges and kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality relations between ranges and kernels (Corollary 2.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A densely defined and closed: (i) N(A) = R(A*)^{⊥}, (ii) N(A*) = R(A)^{⊥}, (iii) N(A)^{⊥} ⊃ R(A*), (iv) N(A*)^{⊥} = R(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These follow from the graph orthogonality and standard duality identities. Some inclusions may be strict in infinite-dimensional/pathological cases; for reflexive spaces equalities improve (closures under weak topologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of operators with closed range (Theorem 2.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A densely defined and closed the following are equivalent: (i) R(A) is closed; (ii) R(A*) is closed; (iii) R(A) = N(A*)^{⊥}; (iv) R(A*) = N(A)^{⊥}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalences are proved by identifying R(A) and R(A*) with sums/intersections of graph subspaces and applying duality theorems (Theorem 2.16). Useful when checking closedness by testing adjoint range or kernel orthogonals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed-range criterion via distance inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: R(A) is closed iff ∃ C such that dist(u, N(A)) ≤ C ||Au|| for all u ∈ D(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical inequality (a priori estimate) gives a method to verify closedness of range; see Exercise 2.14/Remark 18. It is applied by working on the quotient space E/N(A) with graph norm or by direct estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjectivity characterization via adjoint estimates (Theorem 2.20)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A densely defined and closed, the following are equivalent: (a) A is surjective (R(A) = F); (b) ∃ C such that ||v|| ≤ C ||A*v|| ∀v ∈ D(A*); (c) N(A*) = {0} and R(A*) is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The implication (b) ⇒ (a) is the method of a priori estimates: if one can show an estimate ||v|| ≤ C||f|| for any v solving A*v = f, then surjectivity follows. Proofs use the uniform boundedness principle and closedness of A*.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dual surjectivity characterization for A* (Theorem 2.21)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A densely defined and closed, A* is surjective (R(A*) = E*) iff ∃ C such that ||u|| ≤ C ||Au|| ∀u ∈ D(A), and equivalently N(A) = {0} and R(A) is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the natural dual statement to Theorem 2.20 and is proved similarly. It gives criteria to establish injectivity and closedness of range via estimates on A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional simplifications (Remark 20)
rubrics_metrics.description: If dim E < ∞ or dim F < ∞ then A surjective ⇔ A* injective, and A* surjective ⇔ A injective; equivalences hold because ranges are finite-dimensional (hence closed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In finite dimensions many pathologies disappear; in infinite dimensions only the implications A surjective ⇒ A* injective and A* surjective ⇒ A injective hold in general, converses may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: converses fail in infinite dimensions (counterexamples)
rubrics_metrics.description: In general (infinite-dimensional case) the converses of the finite-dimensional equivalences fail: one can construct bounded operators with A* injective but A not surjective (and vice versa); ranges may be dense but not closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple sequence-space example is sketched in the text: operators acting coordinatewise can be injective with dense non-closed range. Use such examples to test hypotheses in arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak (initial) topology construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a set X and collection of maps (φ_i) into topological spaces Y_i, the coarsest (weak/initial) topology making all φ_i continuous is generated by finite intersections of preimages φ_i^{-1}(ω_i) (ω_i open in Y_i) and arbitrary unions thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take finite intersections of the basic preimages, then all arbitrary unions to obtain a topology. Do not reverse the order of operations (finite intersections then arbitrary unions is essential). Basis neighborhoods are finite intersections of φ_i^{-1} of neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the weak topology σ(E,E*)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a Banach space E and f ∈ E*, define φ_f(x) = ⟨f,x⟩. The weak topology σ(E,E*) is the coarsest topology on E making all φ_f continuous (i.e., generated by finite intersections of inverse images of open sets under the linear functionals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The weak topology is weaker (coarser) than the norm (strong) topology. It is metrizable only under special conditions (e.g., on bounded sets when E* separable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential and continuity characterizations for weak topology (Propositions 3.1 and 3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence x_n → x in the weak topology iff φ_i(x_n) → φ_i(x) for every i. A map ψ : Z → X is continuous (weak topology on X) iff each composition φ_i ◦ ψ is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the defining universal properties of the initial/weak topology and are the practical tests used to check weak convergence and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak topology is Hausdorff (separation via Hahn–Banach)
rubrics_metrics.description: σ(E,E*) is Hausdorff: given x1 ≠ x2 there exists f ∈ E* and α ∈ R with ⟨f,x1⟩ < α < ⟨f,x2⟩; the corresponding preimage half-spaces separate x1 and x2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hahn–Banach (geometric form) provides the separating functional; this is a standard density/separation argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic neighborhoods in weak topology (Proposition 3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: A basic neighborhood of x0 in σ(E,E*) has the form V(f1,...,fk;ε) = { x ∈ E : |⟨f_i, x - x0⟩| < ε for i=1..k } where f_i ∈ E* and ε>0; such sets form a neighborhood basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varying ε, k and the f_i's yields the basis. Use these neighborhoods to show properties like lines contained in weak neighborhoods (in infinite-dimensional spaces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of weak convergence (Proposition 3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: (i) x_n ⇀ x iff ⟨f,x_n⟩ → ⟨f,x⟩ ∀ f ∈ E*. (ii) Strong convergence implies weak convergence. (iii) If x_n ⇀ x then (||x_n||) is bounded and ||x|| ≤ lim inf ||x_n||. (iv) If x_n ⇀ x and f_n → f strongly in E*, then ⟨f_n,x_n⟩ → ⟨f,x⟩.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform boundedness to deduce boundedness of sequence norms and Corollary 1.4 to obtain the lim inf inequality. Item (iv) gives a useful mixing limit rule between varying functionals and weakly convergent vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-dimensional equivalence of weak and strong topologies (Proposition 3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: When E is finite-dimensional the weak topology σ(E,E*) coincides with the usual (norm) topology; hence sequences converge weakly iff they converge strongly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses finite basis and coordinate functionals; in finite dimensions all linear functionals separate points and produce the same topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit sphere and unit ball behavior under weak topology (Examples 1 & 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: In infinite-dimensional E the unit sphere S = {||x|| = 1} is never weakly closed: its weak closure equals the closed unit ball B_E. Consequently the open unit ball is never weakly open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The geometric explanation: weak neighborhoods contain lines (huge affine subspaces) so interior points of the ball can be approximated by points on the sphere. Use this to avoid assuming sphere closedness under weak topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex sets: weakly closed ⇔ strongly closed (Theorem 3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: A convex subset C of E is weakly closed iff it is strongly (norm) closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Hahn–Banach separation: a strong-closed convex set can be separated by a functional from any exterior point, producing a weak neighborhood contained in the complement. Consequence: many convex lower-semicontinuity statements transfer to the weak topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mazur's theorem (Corollary 3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x_n ⇀ x weakly, then there exist convex combinations y_n of the x_n's that converge strongly to x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tool: when only weak convergence is available one can often pass to convex combinations to obtain strong convergence; used extensively in variational methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convex l.s.c. strong ⇒ convex l.s.c. weak (Corollary 3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ : E → (−∞,+∞] is convex and lower semicontinuous in the strong topology then φ is lower semicontinuous in the weak topology σ(E,E*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Theorem 3.7 to level sets {x: φ(x) ≤ λ} which are convex and strongly closed; they are then weakly closed, so φ is weakly l.s.c. This is often used to prove existence of minimizers in weak topologies.
